stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Compiled from interviews conducted between 1951 and 1958, the Lowland Speech Atlas recorded how rural speakers in four provinces named ordinary household objects and features of the landscape. In 1964, the atlas's most widely cited finding—that the local words for a skillet, a dragonfly, and a creek bend all shifted at nearly the same river crossings—______ the subject of a conference on whether dialect boundaries trace geography or the routes taken by earlier settlers.
explanation: First, cross out everything between the dashes, which is an appositive explaining the finding. That leaves 'the atlas's most widely cited finding ______ the subject.' The phrase 'the atlas's' is a possessive. It describes the head noun but is not the head noun itself, so the subject is 'finding,' which is singular. That rules out 'were' and 'have been.' Next, look at the time marker. The sentence opens with 'In 1964,' a specific, completed point in the past, and that calls for the simple past. 'Has been' links the action to the present, and that clashes with a fixed past date. Only 'was' gets both the number and the tense right.

A.why: You matched the verb to the nouns right before the blank: the plural list 'a skillet, a dragonfly, and a creek bend' and 'river crossings.' Those all sit inside the dashes. The verb's real subject is the singular 'finding.'

C.why: You found the singular subject correctly, then stopped checking. 'Has been' is singular, but the present perfect cannot go with the fixed past time marker 'In 1964' that opens the sentence. You need the simple past.

D.why: You let the plural nouns inside the dashes set the number, and you also missed the tense. 'Have been' is plural, but the subject 'finding' is singular, and 'In 1964' requires the simple past, not the present perfect.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Gathered in the 1890s from fishing families along the Baltic coast, Seven Tales of the Salt Marsh was among the first folklore collections to print each storyteller's name beside the story they told. Today Seven Tales of the Salt Marsh, along with two companion books of riddles that its editor, Ilse Marten, assembled from the same informants, ______ a standard reference for scholars tracing how coastal legends traveled inland.
explanation: This takes three checks. First, count the finite verbs. The relative clause 'that its editor... assembled' has its own verb, but the main subject still has none, so the blank needs a conjugated verb. That rules out 'remaining.' Second, cross out the interrupter between the commas. 'Along with two companion books of riddles' does not make the subject plural, because only 'and' joins subjects into a plural. Third, look at the subject that is left: Seven Tales of the Salt Marsh. It looks plural, but it is the title of one book, and a title takes a singular verb. The first sentence even says the book 'was among the first.' With a singular subject and 'Today' setting the present tense, the answer is 'remains.'

A.why: You correctly saw that 'along with' doesn't pluralize the subject, but then you read 'Seven Tales' as a plural noun. It is the title of a single book, so it takes the singular 'remains.' The plural nouns 'informants' and 'books' just before the blank add to the pull.

C.why: 'Remaining' is an -ing form, not a conjugated verb. The verb in the 'that' clause belongs to that clause, so the main subject is left with no verb of its own and the sentence becomes a fragment.

D.why: You treated 'along with two companion books' as if it were 'and,' which made the subject plural. Only 'and' does that. The subject is the single title Seven Tales of the Salt Marsh, and 'Today' calls for the simple present.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cordgrass anchors much of the salt marsh along the Georgia coast, and ecologists have long treated it as the system's foundation. Recent fieldwork complicates that picture. The persistence of the cordgrass, along with the fiddler crabs and ribbed mussels that burrow and settle among its roots, ______ on a partnership: the mussels fertilize the grass, and the crabs loosen the mud it grows in.
explanation: Cross out "of the cordgrass" and the whole "along with..." phrase. What's left is "The persistence... depends." The subject is "persistence," which is singular, and the passage is in the present tense ("complicates"), so you need "depends." The word "and" inside "crabs and ribbed mussels" joins nouns in the phrase you crossed out. It doesn't join two subjects, so it doesn't make the subject plural.

A.why: You saw "and" in "crabs and ribbed mussels" and treated the subject as compound. That "and" sits inside the "along with" phrase, and "along with" never makes a subject plural. The subject is "persistence," which is singular.

C.why: You matched the verb to "mussels," the plural noun right before the blank. "Have" is plural, and the true subject, "persistence," is singular.

D.why: "Burrow and settle" belong to the "that" clause, so the main subject "persistence" still has no verb of its own. "Depending" isn't a finite verb, so it leaves the sentence a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Drawn up in 1962, the Halvorsen Plan proposed ringing the city with elevated expressways. Few of its pieces were ever completed. Yet the plan, whose highways, rail spurs, and tower blocks were mostly abandoned after neighborhood protests, still ______ the city: the lots cleared for it remain the largest open parcels downtown.
explanation: Remove the "whose..." clause and the sentence reads "the plan... still shapes the city." The subject is "plan," which is singular, and the colon clause is in the present tense ("remain"), so "shapes" is right. The verb "were" belongs to the "whose" clause. It isn't the main verb, so the sentence still needs one.

A.why: You matched the verb to the plural list "highways, rail spurs, and tower blocks" inside the "whose" clause. The subject is "plan," which is singular.

C.why: You took "were" as the sentence's main verb and thought only a modifier was missing. "Were" belongs to the "whose" clause, so "plan" still needs a finite verb, and "shaping" isn't one.

D.why: "Have" is plural, so it agrees with "tower blocks" or "protests" instead of "plan." The present perfect also doesn't fit with "still" and the present-tense "remain."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most labor surveys interview a fresh sample of households each year, which makes it hard to see how any one worker's pay changes over time. Panel studies take the opposite approach. Following the earnings of the same 4,000 workers through two recessions and dozens of contract negotiations ______ economists to separate the wage loss caused by a layoff from ordinary year-to-year variation.
explanation: There's no comma after "negotiations," so "Following..." isn't an opening modifier. The whole gerund phrase is the subject of the sentence. A gerund phrase is singular, and the passage is in the present tense ("interview," "take"), so you need "allows."

A.why: You matched the verb to "negotiations" or "workers," the plural nouns inside the phrase. The subject is the gerund "Following...," and a gerund subject is singular.

C.why: You read "Following..." as an opening modifier and expected a subject to come later. Without a comma, the gerund phrase is itself the subject, so it needs a finite verb. "Allowing" leaves the sentence without one.

D.why: "Have" is plural, so it agrees with "workers" or "negotiations" and not with the singular gerund subject.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The Eocene lake beds near Republic, Washington, preserve plants in unusual detail because fine volcanic ash settled over leaves before they could decay. In one slab collected in 2019, the ash recorded more than a single species. Pressed flat within its upper layer ______ a seed cone from an early larch and the impressions of two fern fronds, still showing their veins.
explanation: This sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. Ask what is pressed flat. The answer is "a seed cone... and the impressions of two fern fronds." Two things joined by "and" make a plural subject, and the passage is in the present tense ("preserve"), so you need "are."

A.why: You matched the verb to "layer," just before the blank, or stopped at "a seed cone," just after it. The subject is both the cone and the impressions, joined by "and," so it's plural.

C.why: You saw that the subject follows the verb, but you counted only "a seed cone." "Lies" is singular, and the compound subject needs a plural verb.

D.why: You read "Pressed flat..." as an opening modifier and supplied another participle. Inverted sentences still need a finite verb, so "lying" leaves a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the 1790s, Admiralty surveyors sounded the depths of the northern gulf from open boats, often in poor weather. Their results were engraved and bound in London. Harbors and Headlands, a portfolio of forty coastal charts drawn from those soundings, ______ still consulted by local pilots well into the 1880s, long after newer surveys had appeared.
explanation: The subject is a title, "Harbors and Headlands," and a title names one work, so it's singular. The appositive confirms this: it's "a portfolio." The passage describes the 1790s through the 1880s, so you need the singular past tense: "was."

B.why: You saw the "and" in the title, or the plural nouns "charts" and "soundings" before the blank, and treated the subject as plural. A title names a single work, as "a portfolio" confirms.

C.why: "Have" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the singular title. The present perfect also clashes with a time span that ended in the 1880s.

D.why: "Being" isn't a finite verb, so the subject "Harbors and Headlands" is left without a main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When engineers inspected the Ardmore Suspension Bridge after a century of service, they expected to find its main cables badly corroded. They found them nearly intact. The capacity of the cables, each bundled from thousands of galvanized steel wires, to shed rainwater through the gaps between their strands ______ the bridge's long service life, according to the inspection report.
explanation: Cross out "of the cables," the phrase between commas, and the infinitive phrase "to shed... strands." That leaves "The capacity... explains." "Capacity" is singular, and the sentence is in the present tense, so you need "explains."

B.why: You cleared out the interrupter between commas but then matched the verb to "strands" or "cables." The infinitive phrase "to shed... strands" also modifies "capacity," so cross it out too. The subject is "capacity," which is singular.

C.why: "Have" is plural, so it agrees with "wires" or "strands" and not with the singular subject "capacity."

D.why: "Capacity" has no finite verb anywhere in the sentence. "Explaining" doesn't supply one, so the sentence is a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Excavators at the hillfort had assumed that its hearths were used only for cooking. The finds from the 2022 season argue otherwise. The crucible fragments that the team sifted from the ash of the largest hearth, together with a half-finished bronze pin, ______ that metal was being worked on site.
explanation: Cross out the "that the team sifted..." clause and the "together with..." phrase, and "The crucible fragments... suggest" is left. "Fragments" is plural, and the passage is in the present tense ("argue"), so you need "suggest." "Together with" doesn't change the subject's number, so the singular "pin" has no effect on the verb.

A.why: You matched the verb to "pin," the singular noun right before the blank, or to "team" or "hearth" in the relative clause. The subject is "fragments," which is plural.

C.why: "Has" is singular, so it agrees with "pin" or "team" and not with the plural subject "fragments."

D.why: You counted "sifted" as the main verb, but it belongs to the "that" clause. "Fragments" still needs its own finite verb, and "suggesting" isn't one.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Japanese woodblock printers cut each color of a design into a separate block of cherry wood. The wood was durable but not indestructible. The number of clean impressions that a printer could pull from each of the blocks before their finest lines began to blur ______ limited, so publishers often recut popular designs to keep up with demand.
explanation: Cross out "of clean impressions" and the "that..." clause, and "The number... was limited" is left. "The number" is singular, unlike "a number of," which is plural. The passage is in the past tense ("was," "began"), so you need "was."

A.why: You treated "The number of impressions" like "a number of impressions," or matched the verb to "lines," "blocks," or "impressions." With "the," "number" is a singular head noun.

C.why: "Have" is plural, so it doesn't agree with "number." The present perfect also clashes with the past-tense narration.

D.why: You counted "began" as the main verb, but it sits inside the "before" clause. The subject "number" still needs a finite verb, and "being" isn't one.
